transcript.content: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

Well, thank you, doctor. It’s a bit difficult to know exactly where to begin, to be honest. I’m not usually the sort of person who rushes off to a clinic. I spent my entire career working in administration—I have my master's degree, so I’m very used to just analyzing a problem, putting my head down, and pushing through whatever it is. And I’ve been trying to do that lately, just manage things on my own since I retired, but... well, something happened recently that really unsettled me. 

What scared me enough to actually pick up the phone and come in today is that I’ve started having these very dark thoughts. It’s not like me at all. I’ll just be sitting in my living room, doing absolutely nothing of note, and this thought will drift into my head that it would be simpler if I just didn't wake up tomorrow. 

Now, I need you to understand right away, I do not have a plan to harm myself. I would never actually do anything to end my life, I really wouldn't. But just the fact that my brain is even going there, offering up the idea that not waking up would be some kind of relief... it really frightened me. I spent three days just turning it over and over in my mind before I finally admitted I needed to talk to a professional about it, because you just don't expect your own mind to offer up something like that. Especially at my age, you think you have yourself all figured out, and then suddenly you're thinking about how easy it would be to just slip away in your sleep, and it just shakes your foundation a bit, you know?
How long have you been experiencing these dark thoughts?

Well, let me think back... I suppose if I really look at the calendar and trace it all back, it’s been about eight months. Yes, right around eight months. I know the timeline so exactly because it started right after my brother... well, his health took a very sudden turn. 

And it wasn’t just his physical health, you see, his whole behavior changed so abruptly. It was incredibly jarring. We’ve always been quite close, and since I’m the organized one in the family—the one who handles the logistics and the paperwork—I immediately stepped in to help manage his situation. But seeing someone you’ve known your entire life suddenly become so different, so unwell, without any real warning... it was a terrible shock to the system. 

I think the sheer weight of that sudden change just sort of settled over me. At first, I told myself I was just exhausted from dealing with his doctors and trying to sort out his affairs, but the months kept ticking by. And instead of adjusting to this new normal, I just kept having these... these quiet, heavy moments in the evenings where my brain would suggest that just slipping away would be easier than dealing with it all. So, yes, it’s been a solid eight months of this going on, ever since everything with him turned upside down.
Have you noticed any changes in your interest in activities that you used to enjoy over the past eight months?

Well, it's funny you should ask that, because... well, I was just thinking about this exact same thing the other day when I was tidying up the sunroom. You see, I've always been quite an avid watercolor painter. It's something I picked up years ago, actually right around the time I finished my master's degree, as a way to sort of decompress from all the rigid administrative paperwork I was dealing with all day. I even converted our little enclosed porch into a makeshift studio because the morning light in there is just absolutely perfect for capturing the right hues. 

But lately... well, over these past eight months, since everything with my brother happened, it’s just not the same. I try, doctor, I really do try to keep up with it. I’ll go in there, usually on a quiet morning, and I still set out my watercolor things. I'll arrange the brushes by size, fill the water cups, lay out the heavy-pressed paper exactly like I always have for years and years. But then... I don't know, I’ll just sit there. I'll sit there staring at the blank paper, sometimes for twenty or thirty minutes, just looking at it. 

And eventually, I just pack it all up and put it away again. The pleasure I used to feel in the color and the light... it just doesn’t seem to arrive anymore. It’s like the spark of it is entirely gone. I used to get so wonderfully lost in mixing the perfect wash for a sky or finding the exact right tone for a shadow, and now it just feels like I'm going through the motions of a play but I've completely forgotten why I'm on the stage. It's terribly sad, really, because that sunroom used to be my absolute sanctuary, and now it just feels like a room full of useless supplies that I'm just moving back and forth across a desk.
Have you noticed any significant changes in your weight over the past eight months?

Well, weight is a funny thing, isn't it? I mean, at my age, you sort of expect things to shift around a bit anyway. I remember when I first retired, I actually gained a few pounds because I was no longer rushing around the administration building, up and down the stairs to the dean's office, and I was baking more. I used to make these wonderful lemon scones on Tuesdays... but anyway, you're asking about the last eight months. 

I don't think there's been any real change, to be perfectly honest. I mean, my clothes still fit exactly the same. I have this one pair of navy slacks that I always wear when I need to go run errands—they have a very specific clasp on the waistband, so I always know immediately if my weight has fluctuated even a little bit, because that clasp will either pinch or gap. And they feel exactly the same as they did last spring. 

I still go to the grocery store on Thursdays, just like I always have, and I still buy my usual items. I make my toast in the morning, I have my small salad or half a sandwich for lunch, and I make a proper dinner, even if I'm just cooking for myself. I suppose sometimes I might not finish the whole plate quite as enthusiastically as I used to, but I definitely haven't lost any noticeable weight. I stepped on the scale in my bathroom just the other week—it's one of those older dial ones, not the digital kind, so you have to sort of tap it to make sure it's zeroed out properly—and the needle hovered right exactly where it has for the last five or six years. So, no, no significant changes in that department, thankfully. It's just my mind that seems to be heavy, not my body.
Have you been having any trouble sleeping over the past eight months?

Well, sleep... sleep has become quite a complicated ordeal, to be perfectly honest with you. It used to be so simple. I’d read a chapter or two of a good biography—I’ve always preferred biographies over fiction, you see, because I find the actual lived experiences of historical figures so grounding—and then I’d just drift off. But ever since all of this started with my brother, my nights have completely changed their texture. 

When I first get into bed now, I try to keep to my old routine. I fluff the pillows just so, I turn on the little bedside lamp with the green glass shade, but falling asleep is just... it's so uneven. I’ll doze off for a bit, maybe an hour, and then I’ll jolt awake. But the worst part, the part that really wears me down, is what happens in the middle of the night. Almost like clockwork, right around three or maybe four o'clock in the morning, my eyes will just snap open. And the moment I’m awake, my mind just starts racing. 

It’s like a projector switches on in my head, and all it plays are the logistics of the day. I lie there in the dark, staring at the ceiling fan, and I start agonizing over every single detail. Did I fill out that insurance form for him correctly? Should I have made that phone call to the specialist’s office before noon instead of after? Did I say the right thing when the nurse asked about his care plan? It just spins and spins, this endless loop of paperwork and phone calls and second-guessing every decision I’ve made. I try to tell myself to stop, to just breathe and go back to sleep, but the thoughts are so loud. By the time the sun finally comes up and it's time to actually get out of bed, I just feel completely depleted. I drag myself into the kitchen to make my tea, but honestly, I feel as if I haven't rested a single wink all night. It’s just exhausting, doctor, utterly exhausting.
Have you felt a lack of pleasure in activities you used to enjoy, aside from painting?

Well, I know I've gone on a bit about the painting, but honestly... it's just the best example I have of this whole... feeling. Or lack of feeling, I suppose. I mean, I did mention it a moment ago, didn't I? How I'll still go into the sunroom and set out all my watercolor things. I'll arrange everything perfectly, just the way I've done for years, with the brushes lined up and the heavy-pressed paper ready. But then... I just sit there. I'll sit there staring at the blank paper, sometimes for quite a long time, just looking at it. And eventually, I just pack it all up and put it away again. 

Because the pleasure I used to feel in the color and the light... it just doesn’t seem to arrive anymore. It's the same with other things, really, but the painting is where I notice it the most because it used to bring me such profound joy. Now, it's just... flat. Everything feels a bit flat, like the color has been drained out of it, much like my untouched watercolor paper. I try to force it, I really do, but you can't force joy, can you? You can't just mandate that a hobby will make you happy if the spark is simply gone.
Have you been feeling guilty or worthless about anything in particular over the past eight months?

Well, guilt... yes, I suppose guilt is exactly the right word for it. It’s a very heavy thing to carry around. You see, my brother and I, we were always quite close, but you know how life gets. When I was still working at the university, and he had his own routine, we’d mostly just speak on the phone on Sunday afternoons. I’d make my tea, and we’d chat about the news or what he was planting in his garden. 

But lately... especially over these last eight months, I just keep going back over everything. I sit in my chair in the living room and I just replay his entire decline in my head, over and over again, like a tape I can't turn off. I keep telling myself that if I had just been a better sister, if I had only been more attentive, I would have noticed the signs sooner. I think about how he stopped mentioning his tomatoes last summer, or how he sounded just a little bit more vague on the phone, and I think, 'How did you miss that?' 

I feel like I could have prevented some of this, or at least gotten him the right help before things escalated to this point. I mean, I spent my entire career managing complex administrative problems, keeping track of every little detail for the dean, and yet I completely missed what was happening to my own flesh and blood. It just eats away at me, doctor. I should have driven over to his house more often instead of just calling. I should have been paying closer attention. I just feel so terribly useless when I think about how I let him down, and no matter how many times I go over it, the outcome is still the same.
Have you been having thoughts of death or dying frequently over the past eight months, aside from the thoughts of not waking up?

Well, it’s... it’s really just that specific thought, to be perfectly honest. I know you said 'aside from' that, but I really have to emphasize that the thought of not waking up is the primary thing. In fact, it’s the whole reason I’m sitting here in this chair talking to you today. 

I’ve never been the sort of person to dwell on the macabre, you see. During my time at the university, I was known for being immensely practical. You had to be, to manage the dean's schedule and all those departmental crises. So when I started lying there in the dark—usually after the mind-racing I told you about earlier finally exhausts itself—and I caught myself thinking, 'You know, it would just be so much simpler if I simply didn’t wake up tomorrow'... well, it absolutely terrified me. 

It’s not that I want to... I mean, I want to be very, very clear about this, Doctor. I do not have a plan to harm myself. I don't have any sort of scheme or intention to do anything drastic. I could never, ever do something like that, especially not with all the arrangements I still have to manage for my brother. Who on earth would handle his care plan? But the thought just drifts in anyway, this incredibly heavy, exhausting wish for the morning to just... not come. For all the responsibilities to just evaporate while I'm asleep. And having a thought like that, realizing that my mind was actually looking for a way out, even a passive one... it just scared me enough to finally pick up the phone and make this appointment with you.
Have you been feeling more tired or having less energy than usual over the past eight months?

Well, it’s curious you should ask that, because you would think, wouldn't you, with the trouble sleeping and the mind racing I mentioned earlier, that I would be absolutely exhausted during the day. Just dead on my feet. But really... no, I wouldn't say I have less energy, not in the physical sense. 

I mean, I still get up at exactly 6:30 every single morning. I've always been an early riser—back when I was coordinating the dean's office, you simply had to be ahead of the day, you had to be at your desk before the phones started ringing, and I suppose my body just never forgot the habit. So I'm up, I make my bed with the hospital corners, I go downstairs and put the kettle on for my tea... Darjeeling, usually. And I still manage all the daily tasks. I do the grocery shopping on Tuesdays, I clean the house, I handle all the endless phone calls and the mountain of paperwork for my brother's care... there is just so much bureaucracy involved in that, you wouldn't believe the forms I have to fill out. 

So the energy is certainly there to actually *do* the things. I'm not dragging myself around the house or needing to lie down for naps in the afternoon. I keep moving. I just keep putting one foot in front of the other. It's just... well, like I was saying about the painting, the *desire* to do anything is what's missing, the enjoyment of it. But physically? No, I haven't noticed any real drop in my stamina. I just keep going through the motions of the day, even if it all feels a bit hollow. So, no, I'm not more tired than usual.
Have you noticed yourself moving or speaking more slowly than usual over the past eight months?

Moving or speaking more slowly? No, I really don't think so. In fact, if anything, I might be a bit more... well, not rushed, exactly, but certainly not slow. 

You know, when you're managing someone else's entire life—like I am with my brother—you really don't have the luxury of moving slowly. There's always a schedule to keep. The home health aide arrives at exactly 9:00 AM, which means I need to have all of his morning medications sorted out by 8:45, and then there are the phone calls to the insurance company... and let me tell you, if you speak slowly to those insurance representatives, they will just run right over you or put you on hold for another forty-five minutes. You have to be sharp, you have to be quick, you have to have all your reference numbers right there in front of you. 

I've always been a fairly brisk person anyway. At the university, they used to call me 'The Engine' in the dean's office because I was always bustling down the hallways, getting from one meeting to the next. I still walk with purpose, I still talk at my usual clip. I mean, perhaps I might pause a bit more now when I'm trying to remember a specific date for one of those endless medical forms, just because my mind is so cluttered with all the worry, but no, I certainly haven't become sluggish or slow. I just keep moving right along, same as always. If I slowed down, I'm afraid I might just stop altogether, and I simply can't afford to do that right now.
Have you experienced periods of significant depression like this before in your life?

Well, no. No, I haven't. And I suppose that's the thing that makes all of this so incredibly baffling to me, to be quite honest. I have never, ever been someone who gets... well, bogged down like this. 

I mean, I've had difficult times in my life, certainly. Goodness, everyone has at my age. When my husband passed away—oh, that was nearly fifteen years ago now—I grieved, of course I did. But it was a very... a very *practical* grief, if that makes any sense. I threw myself right back into my work at the dean's office. We were right in the middle of restructuring the entire humanities department that year, which was an absolute nightmare of logistics, and I simply didn't have the time to sit around wallowing. I organized the memorial, I sorted out the estate, I kept the university office running smoothly. I felt sad, yes, deeply sad, but I didn't feel this... this awful hollowness. 

And even before that, during my own graduate studies, or when my brother first started showing signs of needing help... I've always just rolled my sleeves up and tackled the problem. People have always leaned on me. I'm the one who fixes things, the one who keeps the trains running on time. So to find myself sitting here, at sixty-eight years old, feeling so entirely depleted of any joy and having those terrible thoughts about just... not waking up... it's completely foreign territory for me. I've never experienced anything remotely like this in my entire life. It's just so entirely unlike me, Doctor, it really is. I've always been the strong one.
Have you felt a lack of interest in social activities or being around other people over the past eight months?

Social activities... yes. Yes, I suppose I have. And that’s another thing that’s just so frustrating to me. Because, as I mentioned, I still take care of all the essentials. The groceries are bought, my brother’s health aides are managed, the bills are paid on time—always on time, I never let a due date slip by. But the extra things, the things that involve actually engaging with other people... I’ve really just pulled back from all of it. 

I used to have this walking group, for instance. Four of us, women I’ve known for years, mostly from my days at the university. We would meet every Thursday morning, rain or shine, and walk the trails over by the botanical gardens, and then we'd always get coffee and a pastry afterward at this little bakery on 4th Street. And I was always the one organizing it, sending the reminder text messages on Wednesday evenings. But lately... oh, for the past several months, I just haven't been going. I tell them I'm too busy with my brother's paperwork, which is partially true, I suppose, but mostly I just can't bring myself to go. 

And the mentoring, too. Even after I retired, I kept up with mentoring some of the younger administrative staff at the dean's office. We’d meet for lunch once a month. They really need that guidance, you know, because university politics can be an absolute minefield if you don't know how to navigate the different department heads and the faculty egos. I always prided myself on helping them find their footing. But I’ve canceled the last three or four lunches with my main mentee, Sarah. 

It's not that I don't care about them, or that I want to be rude. It's just that I can't seem to follow through with the plans anymore. The thought of getting dressed up and sitting across a table from someone for an hour feels insurmountable. And even when I did try to go to the walking group a few months ago, I just couldn't be fully present with them the way I used to be. They would be chatting away about their grandchildren or a book they were reading, and I would just be sitting there, nodding, but feeling a million miles away. I couldn't engage, I couldn't find the energy to contribute to the conversation. It takes so much effort to pretend you're interested when you just feel completely blank inside. So, yes, it just became easier to pull back entirely rather than sit there and not be present.
How long have you been feeling guilty or worthless about your brother's situation?

Well, I suppose it's been building up for a while now, but it's really been consuming me for these past eight months or so. It's just this constant, heavy feeling that I can't seem to shake. I mean, I sit there at the kitchen table, going through his medical files—and there are so many of them, Doctor, stacks and stacks of these blue folders I bought specifically to keep everything organized—and I just keep going back over everything. Over and over. 

I keep going back over my brother’s decline and telling myself that if I had been a better sister, or more attentive, I would have noticed sooner and prevented some of this. You see, he started showing these little signs... forgetting where he put his keys, missing an appointment here and there. And I just brushed it off. I told myself, 'Oh, he's just getting older, we all forget things.' I was so busy with my own life, with the dean's office and the restructuring and everything else, that I just didn't pay close enough attention. 

And now... well, now look at where we are. He needs a home health aide, he can barely manage his own medications, and I just feel this overwhelming guilt. I keep thinking, if I had just stepped in earlier, if I had insisted on taking him to the neurologist two years ago instead of waiting until it became a crisis... maybe things wouldn't be this bad. Maybe he wouldn't be struggling so much. It's my job to take care of him, you know? I'm the organized one, the capable one. I should have seen it coming. I should have done more. And it just makes me feel so incredibly worthless, like I've failed him in the most fundamental way possible. I just can't stop thinking about all the things I should have done differently. It's like a loop playing in my head, day in and day out.
How long have you been feeling guilty or worthless about your role in your brother's life?

Well, like I was just saying a moment ago, it’s really been about eight months now. That was when... well, that's when his health and his behavior just changed so incredibly suddenly. 

Before that, like I mentioned, it was just those little things I was brushing off, telling myself he was just getting a bit older. But eight months ago, it was like a switch flipped. It was so sudden, Doctor. I remember I had just finished setting up a new filing system for my own paperwork—because I always like to keep everything perfectly in order—and I went over to his house to check on him, and it was just... chaos. His behavior was completely different. He was agitated, he wasn't making sense, and his physical health seemed to have just plummeted practically overnight. It wasn't a gradual slope anymore, it was a cliff. 

And that is exactly when this awful, heavy guilt really took root and started suffocating me. Because how could I have missed the edge of the cliff? I’m the one who plans for everything. I spent my entire career at the university anticipating problems before they arose, managing crises, making sure every single contingency was covered for the department. And then, for this to happen so abruptly with my own flesh and blood... well, for these past eight months, ever since that sudden shift, I just haven't been able to forgive myself. I wake up thinking about it, I sit with his blue folders thinking about it, I go to sleep thinking about it. I just can't seem to move past the fact that I let it get to that point before I finally intervened.
How long have you been pulling back from social activities and engagements?

Well, like I was saying before about the guilt, the pulling back from everyone really started at the exact same time. It’s been about eight months. Eight months of just... fading out of my own life, I suppose. 

It all tracks back to when my brother’s health and his behavior took that sudden, awful turn. Before that, I was still keeping up with everything. I was still doing the Thursday morning walks with the girls, still meeting Sarah for lunch to go over all the office politics at the university, still organizing everything for everyone. I was tired, certainly, but I was functioning. I was present. 

But then, eight months ago, when he just seemed to fall off that cliff health-wise... that’s when I stopped being able to manage the social things. It was like all my energy, every single ounce of my capacity to engage with the world, was just instantly redirected into managing his crisis, and into this terrible guilt I’ve been carrying. The walking group texts started going unanswered, or I’d make up an excuse about his paperwork—which, again, I do have a mountain of, all meticulously filed in those blue folders, but that wasn't the real reason. The real reason is that ever since that sudden change with him eight months ago, I just haven't had it in me to sit across from another human being and pretend everything is fine. I just can't do it. The timeline for all of this—the guilt, the isolation, the exhaustion—it all points right back to that exact same moment eight months ago.
Have your feelings of guilt or worthlessness about your brother's situation been present for most of the past eight months or have they varied in intensity over that time?

Well, Doctor, it’s… it’s been pretty much a constant companion, to be perfectly honest. I wouldn’t say it varies much at all. It’s just this steady, relentless drumbeat in the back of my mind. I mean, from the moment I wake up and see those blue folders sitting on the kitchen table—and I keep them right there, right where I can see them, so I don't miss anything important—it just starts all over again. 

I just keep going back over his decline, picking apart every little detail, every conversation, every missed appointment. I sit there with my coffee, and I just tell myself, over and over, that if I had just been a better sister, if I had been more attentive to what was happening right in front of me, I would have noticed sooner. I could have stepped in. I could have prevented some of this from happening. It’s not like it comes and goes, it’s just… always there. It’s like a heavy wool blanket that I can’t take off, even in the dead of summer. I just can’t shake the feeling that I failed him, and that feeling hasn't let up for a single day in these past eight months. Not one single day.
Have you felt a lack of pleasure in activities you used to enjoy consistently over the past eight months?

Well, yes, absolutely. It’s been just as constant as the guilt, I’m afraid. Just a complete and utter flatlining of any joy I used to take in things. 

You know, I’ve always been someone who loved to paint. Watercolors, specifically. I used to spend hours, especially on Sunday afternoons, just getting lost in the washes of color, trying to capture the exact way the light hit the oak tree in my backyard. It was my sanctuary, really. My way of unwinding after a long week at the university. I had this whole routine—I’d brew a pot of Earl Grey, put on some light classical music, maybe some Debussy, and just paint. 

But for these past eight months... it’s just gone. The desire is gone, the joy is gone. I still try, you know. I really do. I’ll go through the motions. I’ll clear off the dining room table—pushing my brother's blue folders to the side, of course—and I’ll set out my watercolor things. I’ll fill the water jars, I’ll lay out the brushes exactly how I like them, I’ll even tape down the paper. But then I’ll just sit there. I sit there staring at the blank white paper, and I wait for that spark, that feeling of excitement about color and light that used to always come... and it just doesn’t arrive. It’s like the part of me that could feel pleasure in something so beautiful is just completely numb now. So, after about twenty minutes of just staring, I end up washing the dry brushes, untaping the pristine paper, and putting it all away again. It’s just exhausting, honestly, trying to force a feeling that simply refuses to come back. So yes, it’s been very consistent for the whole eight months. Just... nothing.
Have you experienced any periods where your depressive symptoms seemed to improve or lighten up at all over the past eight months?

Well, honestly, no. I really haven't. It’s been... it’s been a very steady, very flat line, if you understand what I mean. I keep waiting for a break in the clouds, so to speak, but it just hasn’t happened. 

I remember reading somewhere, years ago when I was doing my graduate work—not in psychology, mind you, but you pick things up—that people often have good days and bad days with these sorts of things. So I’ve been looking for that. I’ve been almost meticulously monitoring myself, the same way I monitor my brother’s endless medical correspondence. I’ll wake up on a Tuesday and think, "Is today the day? Is today the day the weight feels a little lighter?" I’ll go through my morning routine, I’ll make my Earl Grey, I’ll look out at the oak tree, and I’ll try to assess if the grayness has lifted even a fraction of an inch. 

And I’ll think back over the past week, or the past month, trying to pinpoint a moment where I felt a genuine sense of relief, or a genuine spark of... well, of anything other than this exhaustion and this guilt. But every single time I do that inventory, I come up empty. It’s just been this continuous, unbroken stretch. Even on days when the weather is absolutely perfect, or when Sarah calls with some particularly juicy gossip from the faculty senate—things that used to guarantee at least a temporary lift in my mood—it just doesn’t penetrate. It’s like I’m encased in glass. I can see the things that should make me feel better, I can recognize them intellectually, but I can’t actually feel them. So, no, there haven't been any periods of improvement. It’s just been eight solid months of exactly this.
Have there been any times over the past eight months when your symptoms felt significantly worse than they do now?

Well, worse? No, I wouldn't say they've been significantly worse at any point. It’s just... it’s just been this very even, very consistent level of gray. I suppose that’s the best way to describe it. 

You know, I try to think back, trying to see if there was a spike, a time where the guilt or the numbness was unbearable compared to now. Like last month, when my brother had to go in for that extra set of scans, and I was sitting in the waiting room for three hours. The chairs were that awful vinyl that sticks to you, and the magazines were all from 2019, and I just sat there staring at a picture of a casserole, thinking about how I should have pushed him to see a specialist a year ago. I thought, "Is this it? Is this the absolute lowest point?" But honestly, when I really examine it, the feeling in that waiting room wasn't any heavier than the feeling I have sitting at my own kitchen table on a Tuesday morning. 

It’s just this baseline that never shifts. It doesn't dip down into some deeper, darker abyss, but it certainly doesn't rise up into the light either. It’s just... steady. It’s like a hum from a refrigerator that you can't turn off. You get so used to the pitch and the volume of it that you don't even notice if it gets louder, because it just feels like it's been exactly the same volume the entire time. So, no, I haven't had any periods where it felt drastically worse. Just this continuous, unbroken level of... well, of whatever this is.

target_item.manifestation: I still set out my watercolor things sometimes, but I’ll sit there staring at the paper and put it all away because the pleasure I used to feel in color and light just doesn’t seem to arrive.
target_item.reason: The doctor is asking if the patient has felt a lack of pleasure in activities they used to enjoy consistently over the past eight months, which directly corresponds to the Loss_of_Interest symptom.

patient.answer:
Well, yes, absolutely. It’s been just as constant as the guilt, I’m afraid. Just a complete and utter flatlining of any joy I used to take in things. 

You know, I’ve always been someone who loved to paint. Watercolors, specifically. I used to spend hours, especially on Sunday afternoons, just getting lost in the washes of color, trying to capture the exact way the light hit the oak tree in my backyard. It was my sanctuary, really. My way of unwinding after a long week at the university. I had this whole routine—I’d brew a pot of Earl Grey, put on some light classical music, maybe some Debussy, and just paint. 

But for these past eight months... it’s just gone. The desire is gone, the joy is gone. I still try, you know. I really do. I’ll go through the motions. I’ll clear off the dining room table—pushing my brother's blue folders to the side, of course—and I’ll set out my watercolor things. I’ll fill the water jars, I’ll lay out the brushes exactly how I like them, I’ll even tape down the paper. But then I’ll just sit there. I sit there staring at the blank white paper, and I wait for that spark, that feeling of excitement about color and light that used to always come... and it just doesn’t arrive. It’s like the part of me that could feel pleasure in something so beautiful is just completely numb now. So, after about twenty minutes of just staring, I end up washing the dry brushes, untaping the pristine paper, and putting it all away again. It’s just exhausting, honestly, trying to force a feeling that simply refuses to come back. So yes, it’s been very consistent for the whole eight months. Just... nothing.

doctor.intent: Determine the severity of depressive symptoms to differentiate between F32.1 and F33.1
doctor.question: Have you experienced any periods where your depressive symptoms seemed to improve or lighten up at all over the past eight months?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about the course of the depressive symptoms over the past eight months (specifically if there were periods of improvement or lightening of symptoms), which is a question about the longitudinal course/fluctuation of the episode. The symptom profiles cover specific symptoms (depressed mood, loss of interest, sleep, guilt, suicide) and overall duration, but there is no specific item for the episodic course or periods of improvement within the duration.

patient.answer:
Well, honestly, no. I really haven't. It’s been... it’s been a very steady, very flat line, if you understand what I mean. I keep waiting for a break in the clouds, so to speak, but it just hasn’t happened. 

I remember reading somewhere, years ago when I was doing my graduate work—not in psychology, mind you, but you pick things up—that people often have good days and bad days with these sorts of things. So I’ve been looking for that. I’ve been almost meticulously monitoring myself, the same way I monitor my brother’s endless medical correspondence. I’ll wake up on a Tuesday and think, "Is today the day? Is today the day the weight feels a little lighter?" I’ll go through my morning routine, I’ll make my Earl Grey, I’ll look out at the oak tree, and I’ll try to assess if the grayness has lifted even a fraction of an inch. 

And I’ll think back over the past week, or the past month, trying to pinpoint a moment where I felt a genuine sense of relief, or a genuine spark of... well, of anything other than this exhaustion and this guilt. But every single time I do that inventory, I come up empty. It’s just been this continuous, unbroken stretch. Even on days when the weather is absolutely perfect, or when Sarah calls with some particularly juicy gossip from the faculty senate—things that used to guarantee at least a temporary lift in my mood—it just doesn’t penetrate. It’s like I’m encased in glass. I can see the things that should make me feel better, I can recognize them intellectually, but I can’t actually feel them. So, no, there haven't been any periods of improvement. It’s just been eight solid months of exactly this.

doctor.intent: Determine if the patient's depressive symptoms meet the criteria for a persistent depressive disorder (F33.1) or a major depressive disorder (F32.1) by assessing if there have been any periods where the symptoms significantly worsened
doctor.question: Have there been any times over the past eight months when your symptoms felt significantly worse than they do now?

target_item.reason: The doctor is asking about fluctuations in symptom severity (whether they have ever felt significantly worse), which is not specifically covered by any single symptom profile item.

patient.answer:
Well, worse? No, I wouldn't say they've been significantly worse at any point. It’s just... it’s just been this very even, very consistent level of gray. I suppose that’s the best way to describe it. 

You know, I try to think back, trying to see if there was a spike, a time where the guilt or the numbness was unbearable compared to now. Like last month, when my brother had to go in for that extra set of scans, and I was sitting in the waiting room for three hours. The chairs were that awful vinyl that sticks to you, and the magazines were all from 2019, and I just sat there staring at a picture of a casserole, thinking about how I should have pushed him to see a specialist a year ago. I thought, "Is this it? Is this the absolute lowest point?" But honestly, when I really examine it, the feeling in that waiting room wasn't any heavier than the feeling I have sitting at my own kitchen table on a Tuesday morning. 

It’s just this baseline that never shifts. It doesn't dip down into some deeper, darker abyss, but it certainly doesn't rise up into the light either. It’s just... steady. It’s like a hum from a refrigerator that you can't turn off. You get so used to the pitch and the volume of it that you don't even notice if it gets louder, because it just feels like it's been exactly the same volume the entire time. So, no, I haven't had any periods where it felt drastically worse. Just this continuous, unbroken level of... well, of whatever this is.

opening_question.question: Hello, welcome to the clinic. What brings you in to see me today?

final_diagnosis.reason: The patient's symptoms of persistent feelings of guilt, worthlessness, lack of pleasure in activities, and recurrent thoughts of death, which have been present for over eight months, meet the criteria for a Major Depressive Disorder. The patient's age, the sudden onset of symptoms following a significant life event (brother's health decline), and the absence of any previous depressive episodes suggest a diagnosis of Major Depressive Disorder, Recurrent, which is best represented by the ICD-10 code F33.1.
